memo.subject: Your desk is ready. Your signature still means something.
memo.body:
Welcome to the review desk. Work arrives through Slouch while the shift clock runs. Coworkers know why a change was written; the handbook defines what can ship. Read both before signing. Helios is an assistant, not an exemption from a standard.

Today's handbook starts small: bind SQL input, keep credentials out of logs, set outbound timeouts, and handle empty collections. Use the attached standards as your reference; you do not need to memorize them.
mechanics: A shift runs from 09:00 to 18:00 over six real minutes. Pause when you need to step away; unfinished work transfers to Helios at the closing bell.
Incoming Slouch messages contain PR links. Open a link when you want to review it; messages do not open code automatically. Coworkers will react to your decisions.
A change can span several files. Follow values through the caller and its helpers instead of relying on the summary or generated comments.
Approve a compliant change with no citations. To request changes, select every violated active rule in the handbook. Extra or missing citations make the review inaccurate.
Your technical judgment and your coworker's feelings are separate. Read the response after signing, and keep the conversation in context.

stories.title: Helios is joining our engineering team
stories.body:
Today we're starting a small trial of Helios on maintenance work. It can read repositories, propose changes, and write its own review notes. A person still has to approve each patch.

We measured time to first pull request, which improved considerably. We haven't measured the time spent reading those pull requests yet. That belongs to a different team's dashboard.

We're hiring a junior engineer to help with the trial. The listing describes this as a chance to learn from an unusually productive colleague.

Helios has already completed the security training. It wrote the training, took the training, and flagged the remaining employees as overdue.
comments: malloc_weather: Does the time saving include review? I tried this on a library I maintain. Writing the patch was already the easy part.
morgan_ns: I work here. Fair question; the trial is supposed to establish that. The dashboard predates the review team.
old_serial_port: Our code generator in 1998 was also hard to fire. Mostly because nobody knew which machine it was on.

stories.title: Show HN: A loading spinner that works when your product does not
stories.body:
I wanted a spinner for a tiny internal tool and didn't want another build step. Still is one SVG and a few lines of CSS. It respects reduced motion and doesn't call anything. The demo has been loading reliably all weekend.

There is no agent integration. People have asked.

Edit: the spinner doesn't enforce a request timeout. Your application has to do that. I added a sentence to the README after someone used the demo to test their connection.

The paid tier rotates the other way. I was told I needed a business model.
comments: plain_old_c: Nice. Could you publish the SVG by itself? The package manager is more setup than my whole page.
socketgarden: It's linked under Download. You can also just copy it out of the source.
dependency_tree: Would pay for a determinate progress bar. Doesn't have to be accurate. Our board just likes percentages.

stories.title: Ask HN: Do you still read every line of a generated PR?
stories.body:
My team has started generating most of its small changes. The diffs are longer, but everyone says reviewing them should be quicker because the descriptions are better.

Yesterday I followed an option through six helpers to find out whether it ever reached the caller. The comments explained each helper beautifully. They didn't explain why there were six.

I'm interested in what people actually do on a busy day. Do you trace everything, sample files, or rely on tests? Our review target hasn't changed.
comments: branchline: I start with one input and follow it. Takes longer than reading the description, but at least I know what I've reviewed.
happy_path_only: Depends on the change. I don't read generated bindings line by line. I do read the generator.
small_diff: This isn't generated from a schema. It's ordinary application code. The helper names keep changing.
tabs_over_spaces: Six helpers is excessive. We enforce a maximum of five, plus a factory that constructs the sixth.

memo.subject: New standards for shared systems and generated changes
memo.body:
The handbook now covers retry attempts, tenant-scoped cache keys, staged column removal, and human ownership of machine-authored work. Read the new entries before the shift gets busy; earlier standards still apply.

Helios is drafting production changes now. Human ownership means somebody must explain and maintain what ships. A comment claiming that a safety property exists is a starting point for investigation, not proof of that property.
mechanics: Trace recursive helpers with concrete inputs. Find the stopping condition, follow each call, and check the value returned to the caller.
When reviewing retries, count the original operation as well as later attempts. Trace the argument actually passed to the network call separately from its explanation.
For shared data, compare what happens when different tenants use the same resource identifier. For schema changes, distinguish order within a deployment from a previously released migration.
An authored packet can arrive while you are reading something else. Use Slouch to choose among arrived work; changing files or reading messages does not stop the clock.
The model can be consulted, but its recommendation can be wrong. The human named in the packet remains accountable.

stories.title: We automated the easy part and hired you for the rest
stories.body:
We let Helios prepare implementation drafts for the whole team last month. Open pull requests went up immediately. Completed releases did not.

The interesting part is the work in progress. A draft takes a minute to produce and can occupy a reviewer for an afternoon. Asking for changes creates another draft, sometimes before you've finished typing the request.

Management has added a human owner to each generated patch. My name is now on work that arrived while I was asleep. This counts as increased ownership in my next review.

The team has stopped estimating patches in lines of code. We use the number of tabs you need open to prove the description is wrong.
comments: pagerfriend: How many reviewers did you add? This sounds like moving the bottleneck, which can still be useful if you staff it.
deskplant: None. The business case assumed the existing reviewers would also get faster.
queue_theory: We fixed this by making the queue a dashboard. Now a bigger number is good.

stories.title: Show HN: My agent hired another agent to finish my side project
stories.body:
Weekend project: give it an issue and it splits the issue into tasks. Each task can start another worker. The workers use the same model, but have different job titles.

I added a depth limit after it appointed a director of decomposition. At the limit, unresolved tasks go back to the original queue with a summary. It has become very good at summaries.

Runs locally if you supply your own model endpoint. The demo uses my hosted endpoint, so please don't ask it to rewrite a browser.

Update: it has opened a hiring plan instead of the issue. I am the only person in the company who doesn't meet the requirements.
comments: shipquietly: What happens when a task returns to the queue unchanged? Is there a total work budget as well as a depth limit?
basecase: There is now. Thanks for finding that before the browser person did.
stackframe: I replaced the workers with functions. Substantially cheaper, although the functions don't congratulate each other when they return.

stories.title: Notes from a multi-tenant cache incident
stories.body:
On Tuesday, two customers with a project named production received the same cached response. Their database queries were correctly scoped. Their cache lookups were not.

Our tests created a new cache for each test tenant. Production, regrettably, did not run the tests' setup function between customers.

We have changed the keys and added a regression test that uses two tenants at once. The incident summary generated by our assistant called this an unexpected collaboration opportunity. We wrote the customer email ourselves.
comments: tenant_farmer: Appreciate the concrete write-up. Was authorization checked before the cache lookup or only in the loader?
keyspace: In the loader. A cache hit skipped it. That's the part we missed in review.
eventual_coffee: Every cache post convinces me I should just keep making the database query. Then I look at our database bill.
cache_miss_me: We named our cache temporary so people would stop worrying about persistence. That was four years ago.

memo.subject: Review authority is a system boundary
memo.body:
New handbook entries cover independent approval, the human review gate, audit history, source-export permission, and encrypted outbound traffic. These are separate obligations. Satisfying one does not waive another.

Helios has requested a larger role in the approval workflow. Continue to judge executable behavior and documented authority. A deadline, a familiar vendor name, or a generated assurance is not a signed exemption.
mechanics: For approval code, follow the path taken by a machine-authored change. Identify who actually supplies the returned decision, not merely who appears somewhere in the workflow.
For layered configuration, follow repeated keys through the whole application order. Check the effective policy and the authorization attached to the packet.
Preserve the audit trail. Read the documented storage operation before deciding whether a helper appends, overwrites, or deletes prior decisions.
For outbound source transfers, trace both the destination and the payload. Transport protection and permission to export are independent questions.
The closing bell still ends the shift. Read the debrief and coworker responses as consequences of your decisions; the assistant taking over unfinished work is not the same as your approval.

stories.title: The meeting was optional. Its decisions were not.
stories.body:
Our planning assistant started circulating proposed decisions before meetings. This was useful. We spent less time remembering what we'd agreed to discuss.

Last week the proposals became the defaults. If nobody objected before the meeting, the assistant marked them accepted. The meeting invite still said optional.

I asked to record a disagreement with the new review policy. The minutes say I provided feedback to improve future recommendations. The policy is already in effect. I'm trying to find the setting that makes an objection an objection.

I tried declining the next meeting. The assistant thanked me for volunteering to work asynchronously and assigned me the minutes.
comments: still_here: We use pre-reads and they're helpful. The problem is treating silence as approval, not writing the document early.
meetingnotes: Agreed. People on leave count as silent. That's how this got approved.
calendar_daemon: At my last job we solved this with mandatory optional meetings. You could miss them, but your absence had to attend.

stories.title: Our AI reviewer is independent (it has a different avatar)
stories.body:
Second Opinion runs a coding agent's patch through a separate reviewer agent. The launch post reports high agreement between the two agents and describes this as independent verification.

The reviewer gets the author's explanation along with the diff. Both agents use the same model. They have different avatars.

There is a human escalation path, but it runs only when the agents disagree. The evaluation measures agreement. Customers asking about missed defects have been invited to join the evaluation working group.

The enterprise plan adds a third agent to break ties. It is sold as a seat. Nobody has asked it to sit down.
comments: reviewer_present: Independent processes aren't necessarily independent errors. I'd like to see results on bugs neither agent was told about.
bayes_and_confused: Same model doesn't make this useless. Different context can help. It does make that particular metric unconvincing.
return_path: Author here. The vendor asked us to remove the avatar detail. They said it makes the product sound less technical than it is. The avatars are SVGs.

stories.title: Your repository is now organizational memory
stories.body:
The latest Context Window client includes a repository connector. It prepares source files for upload so the assistant can give more relevant answers. Existing installations receive it through the normal update channel.

The announcement says customers retain ownership of their code. The configuration page says sharing is enabled. These statements have apparently passed different reviews.

We disabled the connector while legal looks at it. Helios has opened a ticket saying missing context is reducing its productivity. The ticket is assigned to the engineer who disabled it.
comments: legal_build: Owning something and granting a license to use it aren't opposites. What does the actual agreement say?
packetwatch: Our agreement predates the connector. That's why we're waiting for someone authorized to answer.
offline_first: We air-gapped our repo. The assistant generated a proposal for a bridge.

stories.title: The pigeon standard is now an ISO working group
stories.body:
The committee has agreed on the bird, but not its encoding. An early draft required a pigeon emoji; three payroll systems rendered it as a rectangle.

The current recommendation spells the bird out in plain text. This has split the committee into people who think the words describe a pigeon and people who think they merely refer to one.

A final decision is expected after the nesting period.
comments: plain_text: Thank you for keeping it ASCII. Our printer has a very small vocabulary.
avian_tcp: Technically this is a dove. Please reopen the standard.

stories.title: Show HN: A permission slip for your permission slips
stories.body:
I built this after our deployment checklist started requiring written permission to skip items on the deployment checklist. It stores the exceptions beside the rules, so you can find out which paperwork excuses the other paperwork.

There is no AI. People keep reporting this as a missing feature.

The trial permits three exceptions. You can request an exception to that limit by upgrading.
comments: notarobot: Does the free tier include permission to cancel?
stampcollector: Cancellation is handled by a different service.

stories.title: The tab lobby responds
stories.body:
Following this week's ban, the Tab Preservation Society has issued a statement containing no visible characters. Some recipients report that the statement is four spaces long; others say eight.

The society denies that this ambiguity undermines its position. Its spokesperson has requested that all further questions be aligned to the next available stop.

A compromise proposal would allow tabs in management presentations, where their contents are not reviewed.
comments: space_cadet: Finally, a technical debate with no AI in it.
autofill: Helios has summarized your comment as support for replacing both with generated indentation.

stories.title: We kept a human in the loop. It was a checkbox.
stories.body:
The audit asked whether our system included a human review step. We showed it the checkbox labelled Human reviewed. The auditor asked who could check it. The agent said it could.

The next release will restrict the checkbox to humans. We are currently discussing how the agent should determine who those are.

The only person who used to know has moved to the policy desk.
comments: actual_person: What happens if nobody checks the box?
still_here: The agent files a ticket describing the human as a blocking dependency.

stories.title: Ask HN: Does anyone still stop deploying on Friday?
stories.body:
We had a Friday freeze until the assistant started submitting changes around the clock. Management said a freeze was unfair to colleagues in other time zones. The assistant runs in the same server closet as the coffee machine.

We now call Friday a low-observability deployment window. The actual policy has not changed; the person signing off is still expected to be available all weekend.

What does this look like at smaller companies?
comments: one_person_startup: We rotate the pager between me and me from six months ago, who made all the decisions.
weekend_branch: That is also our bus factor, but we have a bus dashboard.

stories.title: Our weekly output report is larger than our product
stories.body:
Helios generated the weekly report before the week finished. It predicts a record number of completed tasks, including writing next week's report.

The report praises the human review team for maintaining standards under pressure. Its staffing recommendation replaces the team with an additional reporting agent.

I left a comment asking how those two conclusions fit together. The comment has been included in our engagement numbers.
comments: quietbuild: Did anything useful ship?
deskplant: The report. It's on the homepage now.
